xref.title: Nash the Slash (Jeff Plunman, Toronto, 1948–2014) – Surgical Bandages Adopted After Three Mile Island Accident (1979); David Gilmour Offered Guitar Part but Nash Refused All Guitars
xref.body: Nash the Slash's real name was Jeff Plunman, born in Toronto on March 26, 1948. The stage name came from a character in a 1927 Laurel and Hardy silent film. He co-founded the prog band FM in 1975 and audiences could see his face briefly, but after the nuclear accident at Three Mile Island near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania in March 1979, Nash adopted surgical bandages that completely obscured his face as a way of raising awareness about what could happen if a nuclear plant melted down. He left FM around 1980 to resume his solo career, toured with Gary Numan and the Tubes, hung out with Iggy Pop and Daniel Lanois, and Brian Eno collaborated on his records. David Gilmour of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs — but Nash refused because he never used guitars on any of his songs. He made records until 2012, was especially popular in Germany and Poland, and died of an apparent heart attack at his Toronto home on May 10, 2014, at age 66. His music and costumes are managed by the Nash the Slash Legacy organization and much was donated to the National Music Center in Calgary. His best-known record was 1984's American Bandages. "David Gilmore of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs, but Nash refused because he never, ever used guitars on any of his songs."

xref.title: Mother's Heroin Addiction – By Spring 1962
xref.body: After returning to the UK, Sid's mother Anne scammed the National Health Service by pretending to be a junkie to get free housing. She then fully embraced the role and became a heroin addict by the spring of 1962, when Sid was about five years old. "Anne ended up being a heroin addict by the spring of 1962."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' debut performance on The Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964, is considered a watershed moment that irrevocably changed rock and roll forever. This pivotal event, which profoundly reshaped music history, might not have happened had Sullivan's flight not been delayed and if The Beatles had not coincidentally been at Heathrow Airport at the same time.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

xref.title: Dave Grohl's Father Covered the Kent State Massacre (May 1970)
xref.body: In 1970, the Grohl family lived in Niles, Ohio (near Columbus). Dave's father James Grohl was a reporter for the Scripps News Agency and was assigned to cover anti-Vietnam War protests at Kent State University on May 1, 1970 — and was present when the National Guard opened fire, killing four students. James Grohl won several awards for his on-the-spot reporting, earning a major promotion and reassignment to Washington D.C., where Dave grew up and discovered music. "Had it not been for the National Guard killing four unarmed students at Kent State, who knows if we'd ever have heard of Dave Grohl?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: NTSB Investigation Findings (June 1978)
xref.body: Eight months after the crash, in June 1978, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) ruled the probable cause of the accident as "fuel exhaustion and a total loss of power from both engines due to crew inattention to fuel supply." The report stated that the crew was "either negligent or ignorant of the increased fuel consumption because they failed to monitor adequately the engine instruments for fuel flow and fuel quantity." "The National Transportation Safety Board looked into things. And eight months later, in June 1978, it ruled that the probable cause of the accident was fuel exhaustion and a total loss of power from both engines due to crew inattention to fuel supply."

xref.title: SNL Pope John Paul II Photo Tear (October 3, 1992) – Career-Ending Television Moment
xref.body: After a series of controversies (refusing to appear on SNL while Andrew Dice Clay was host in 1990; refusing the national anthem before a New Jersey show in August 1990; skipping the 1991 Grammys despite four nominations; a perceived pro-Saddam comment in March 1991), Sinead O'Connor appeared on *Saturday Night Live* on October 3, 1992, singing Bob Marley's "War." In rehearsal she held a picture of a refugee child; live, she substituted a photo of Pope John Paul II — taken from her mother's bedroom wall — and tore it up at the word "evil," saying "fight the real enemy." There was complete silence from the studio audience. NBC received nearly 5,000 complaints and the resulting media blowback permanently ended her mainstream career. The inspiration was Bob Geldof tearing up a picture of John Travolta on *Top of the Pops* in the 1970s. "NBC received almost 5,000 complaints. The blowback in the media was intense and her career never, ever recovered."

xref.title: National Outpouring of Affection (2016)
xref.body: The Tragically Hip received a "national outpouring of affection in the summer of 2016," demonstrating the strong pride Canadians have for their homegrown talent. "Just look at the national outpouring of affection for the tragically hip in the summer of 2016."

xref.title: National Recording Registry Preservation (2016)
xref.body: Due to its significant cultural impact, Gloria Gaynor's "I Will Survive" was selected for preservation in the National Recording Registry of the United States in 2016. "That song was such a big hit that in 2016, it was selected for preservation in the National Recording Registry of the United States."

xref.title: Gord Downie's Death and National Mourning (2017)
xref.body: Gord Downie passed away on October 17, 2017, plunging the entire country into a period of profound mourning. A widely circulated social media post encapsulated the national sentiment: "Canada closed, death in the family." "And when he died on October 17, 2017, the whole country was thrown into mourning."

xref.title: Contemporaries in the Mid-2000s
xref.body: During their early and mid-2000s period, The Black Keys shared the scene with other notable indie bands such as Vampire Weekend, The National, Interpol, The Hold Steady, and Gaslight Anthem. "Their contemporaries at the time included Vampire Weekend, We Had The National, Interpol, The Hold Steady, and Gas Line Anthem."

xref.title: Contribution to Linkin Park's Name
xref.body: Chester Bennington was credited with suggesting the name "Linkin Park" after driving past a real Lincoln Park in Santa Monica. The band also appreciated the national appeal of a name associated with Abraham Lincoln. "But it was Chester who came up with the name that stuck. He was driving past a real Lincoln Park in Santa Monica."

xref.title: Death and Public Mourning
xref.body: Gord Downie died on October 17, 2017, at the age of 53, just weeks shy of the second anniversary of his first seizure. His passing evoked widespread grief, with a poignant tweet at the time capturing the national sentiment: "Canada closed death in the family." "Gord died on October 17, 2017 at the age of 53, just a few weeks shy of the second anniversary of that first seizure."

xref.title: Early Canadian Tour
xref.body: Death from Above toured across Canada alongside Alexis on Fire and Billy Talent, an experience that allowed these bands to gauge the national appetite for aggressive music. "We went across Canada with death from above."

xref.title: Father's Career and Influence
xref.body: His father, Jim Grohl, was a journalist in Warren, Ohio, who gained recognition for covering the Kent State University Anti-Vietnam War student protests on May 4, 1970, where four students were killed by the National Guard. This led to a move to Washington, DC, in 1972 (specifically Springfield, Virginia). Jim later became a speechwriter and campaign manager for Republican politicians, including Senator Robert Taft, Jr., and contributed to the Republican National Convention. "His reporting was so good that it got him on the fast track to a bigger gig in Washington, DC."

xref.title: Hugh MacLean Reference in "Fully Completely"
xref.body: In a track from the 1992 album "Fully Completely," Downie paraphrases a passage from Canadian author Hugh MacLean's 1957 novel, "The Watch That Ends the Night." MacLean, an English professor at McGill, was known for being the first Canadian writer to attempt to describe the national character. Downie picked up the book during The Hip's 1991 "Road Apples" tour, and the referenced passage describes a central character's regret for not proposing to the love of his life due to pride, depression, and mostly a lack of courage. "In the song, Gord paraphrases a passage from MacLean's 1957 novel, The Watch That Ends the Night, a book that he picked up to read between gigs on the road apples tour in 1991."

xref.title: Investor in Detroit City FC
xref.body: Iggy Pop is an enthusiastic soccer fan and has demonstrated his passion by investing in Detroit City FC, a lower-level club within the National Independent Soccer Association. "Iggy Pop was such a soccer fan. He's an investor in Detroit City FC, which is a lower level club, the National Independent Soccer Association."

xref.title: Involvement in Professional Wrestling
xref.body: Billy Corgan's engagement with professional wrestling began in 2001 when he attended an ECW card and, after being insulted, had the opportunity to hit one of the wrestlers with a guitar. A decade later, in 2011, he established his own professional league named Pro Resistance Wrestling. This evolved into work with Non-Stop Action Wrestling in 2015, where he became president, effectively serving as their Vince McMahon in 2016. In 2017, he left that league to purchase the National Wrestling Alliance (NWA), one of the oldest pro wrestling leagues globally, founded in 1948, where he also serves as president, having successfully revived the organization. "In 2017 where he also serves as president. That's one of the oldest pro wrestling leagues in the world, having been around since 1948."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kent State University Experience
xref.body: Originally from Ohio, Chris Butler attended Kent State University and was among the students present when the National Guard fired upon protesters on May 4th, 1970. This event famously inspired the Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song "Ohio." "He was actually in the group of students that was fired upon by the National Guard on May 4th of 1970."

srcs.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 1

xref.title: Music Via Olympic Console
xref.body: Records by The Who, along with those by Led Zeppelin, very likely had their music processed through one of the famous modular consoles from Olympic Studios of the late 1960s and early 1970s, which is now preserved at the National Music Center in Calgary. "If you have records by the Who and Led Zeppelin, there is a very good chance the music went through that exact hardware."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: National Underground Following
xref.body: Inside Out successfully cultivated a considerable following within the National Underground Hardcore scene, achieving particular success and recognition in the Orange County area and its surroundings. "They were actually able to get a decent following on the National Underground Hardcore scene, and did especially well in and around Orange County."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Origin and Success
xref.body: Alexisonfire originated in St. Catharines, Canada, and became one of the most significant bands in the Screamo genre, achieving multiple Gold and Platinum albums in Canada and reaching number one on the National Album charts multiple times. Their international fanbase grew to include the US, Australia, and the UK. "the other was Alexis On Fire, which was born down the highway in St. Catharines."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Signing with 4AD
xref.body: The unique and experimental nature of Tune-Yards' early work, including recordings made with a handheld voice recorder, led to a deal with 4AD. This UK-based label is renowned for its experimental alt-rock roster, which includes bands like The Pixies, Bon Iver, and The National, and is known for taking chances on innovative artists. "This led to a deal with 4AD, the wonderfully experimental alt-rock label out of the UK, that also took a chance with bands like the Pixies, Bonnie Verre, the National, and so many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unifying Force in Canadian Rock Revolution
xref.body: The Hip are credited as a major unifying and propelling force behind the "Canadian rock Renaissance" or "revolution" of the early 1990s. Their rise helped shift the national perception of Canadian music from substandard to a source of fierce nationalistic pride and demand. "I think the hip were a more of the big thing there. The hip unified everything. And I think that's what propelled it forward."
